a: The maximum amount of data that can be sent in a given time
The length of the network cable
The number of devices on the network
The delay before data arrives
tasks.fb: Bandwidth is how much data can travel per second. The delay before data arrives is latency, a different factor.

tasks.q: What unit is bandwidth usually measured in?
a: Megabits per second (Mbps)
Milliseconds (ms)
Megabytes (MB)
Gigahertz (GHz)
tasks.fb: Bandwidth is a rate, so it is measured in bits per second. Milliseconds measure latency; megabytes measure file size.

tasks.q: Why does a network slow down when more people use it at the same time?
a: They all share the same bandwidth, so each person gets less
Each new user deletes some of the data
The cables get longer
The router changes its IP address
tasks.fb: The available bandwidth is split between everyone using it at that moment.

tasks.q: Which change would most help a network that is slow when everyone uses it at once?
a: Increasing the network's bandwidth
Moving the printer to another room
Changing everyone's passwords
Turning the computers' screens down
tasks.fb: More bandwidth means each user's share is bigger, even when lots of people are online.

tasks.q: Which connection usually offers the highest bandwidth over long distances?
a: Fibre optic cable
UTP copper cable
Wi-Fi
Bluetooth
tasks.fb: Fibre carries data as light, with very high bandwidth over many kilometres.

tasks.q: Why is a wired connection usually more reliable than Wi-Fi?
a: Wireless signals weaken with distance and are blocked by walls, but a cable isn't affected in the same way
Cables are always made of glass
Wi-Fi only works outdoors
Wired connections don't use any bandwidth
tasks.fb: Walls, distance and interference all weaken Wi-Fi. A cable delivers a steadier connection.

tasks.q: What happens when a packet is damaged or lost on the way?
a: It has to be sent again, which slows the network down
It is deleted and never needed
The network speeds up to make up for it
The switch changes its MAC address
tasks.fb: Resending damaged data uses extra bandwidth and time, so a high error rate slows everything down.

tasks.q: Which is most likely to increase the error rate on a Wi-Fi network?
a: Interference from other devices, such as microwave ovens and nearby Wi-Fi networks
Using a strong password
Adding more RAM to the laptop
Switching to fibre optic cable
tasks.fb: Other radio signals can interfere with Wi-Fi and damage data, so more of it has to be resent.

a: The delay between data being sent and it arriving
The amount of data that can be sent per second
The number of people using the network
The number of errors in the data
tasks.fb: Latency is a delay, measured in milliseconds. The amount of data per second is bandwidth.

tasks.q: For which activity does low latency matter most?
a: Playing a fast-paced online game
Downloading a film to watch later
Sending an email
Backing up files overnight
tasks.fb: In a game, every delay between pressing a button and seeing the result is noticeable. A download just needs to finish eventually.

tasks.q: Why could more CCTV cameras slow down the school network?
a: Each camera streams video all the time, using up bandwidth that everyone shares
Cameras delete files from the server
Cameras change the school's IP address
Cameras make the Wi-Fi password longer
tasks.fb: Video is a lot of data. More cameras means more of the shared bandwidth is used up, all day and night.

tasks.q: The new cameras will be outside, a long way from the building. What is the best advice?
a: Use cabled connections if possible, as Wi-Fi outdoors may be slow and unreliable, and check the network has enough bandwidth
Connect them by Bluetooth
Plug them into the printer
Nothing needs checking, because distance doesn't affect networks
tasks.fb: Distance weakens Wi-Fi and increases errors. The manager should also check bandwidth and server storage for the extra video.

tasks.q: Match each help desk problem to the factor causing it.
pairs: Downloads slow right down every lunchtime, when 300 students go online
A 10 Mbps connection can't stream several HD videos at once
A laptop at the far end of the building keeps losing its Wi-Fi
Packets are corrupted near heavy machinery and keep being resent
Online gamers notice a delay between pressing a button and the action happening
tasks.fb: These are the five factors in the specification. In the exam, name the factor and explain how it slows the network.

info.title: Bits and bytes
info.text: Broadband speeds are given in megabits per second (Mbps), but file sizes are in megabytes (MB). There are 8 bits in a byte, so a 100 Mbps connection downloads at most about 12.5 MB each second.

info.title: Why evenings are slower
info.text: Home broadband often slows down in the evening, when lots of people in the same area are streaming at the same time. It's the number-of-users factor on a bigger scale.

info.title: 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz?
info.text: Wi-Fi uses two main radio bands. 5 GHz is usually faster, but its signal doesn't travel as far or pass through walls as well as 2.4 GHz.

info.title: Spotting damaged data
info.text: Packets carry extra check information. The receiving device checks it, and if the data doesn't match, the packet is sent again.

info.title: Distance adds delay
info.text: Data sent to Australia and back typically takes around a quarter of a second, however much bandwidth you have. Gamers call this delay 'ping'.

info.title: Video is heavy
info.text: An HD camera can send several megabits of video every second, all day and night. Ten cameras can use as much bandwidth as a whole class streaming videos.
